1889-1916

Caption This

The Progressive Era

12

How this works (15–20 minutes)

  1. Look at each of the 5 images. Read the “What you’re looking at” line.
  2. Write a short, funny caption, like a meme. Pick a caption style if you want one.
  3. Then write 2–3 sentences about what is really going on. Use at least one key term from the lesson. Type the key term in English, exactly as shown.
  4. Save Progress any time. When all 5 are done, press Finished and upload the file to Canvas.

Keep it respectful: make the joke about the company, the idea, or the situation. Never joke about workers, children, immigrants, enslaved or freed people, Native peoples, anyone’s race or religion, or people who were hurt.

Image 1 of 5

Jane Addams at Hull House

Not done

What you’re looking at: A black-and-white photograph from Norton Ch. 20. An older woman with gray hair and a pearl necklace stands with a little girl and four young women in matching dresses. Norton says she is Jane Addams, who started Hull House, a settlement house in Chicago.

Heads up: Real people, including a child, are in this photo. Aim your joke at the idea of one big house with a nursery, a gym, a coffeehouse, and a public bath. Never joke about the girls, the poor, or immigrants.

  • Who is the older woman looking at? What mood do you see on the faces?
  • Norton says Hull House had a nursery, music lessons, and a public bath. How could that help a neighborhood?
Pick a caption style (optional)

Image 2 of 5

“Votes for us when we are women!”

Not done

What you’re looking at: A colorized photograph from the first page of Norton Ch. 20. An automobile is covered in flags and bunting. Women and many young girls ride in it. Some hold signs that say “Votes for us when we are women.”

Heads up: Real people, many of them children, are in this photo. Aim your joke at the flags, the bunting, or the car packed with signs. Never joke about the girls, the women, or the right to vote.

  • Read the signs. What do they ask for?
  • Why would a group decorate a car with so many flags?

Image 3 of 5

The Tenement Workshop exhibit

Not done

What you’re looking at: A brown-toned photograph from Norton Ch. 20. A wall display shows clothes and a glove with signs that list what workers were paid. A framed photo says “Products of the Tenement Workshop.” Signs say “Glove Finishing,” “Chiffon Applique,” and “Infants Dress.” Norton says this was a 1908 exhibit in New York.

Heads up: This is a serious one. The exhibit is about real workers, including children, who sewed in crowded homes for very low pay. Write one clear, serious line. No jokes about the workers or the children. Look at how the exhibit tries to change people’s minds.

  • Read the sign on the Infants Dress. How many hours is the working day? What is the day’s pay?
  • Look at the small photo at the lower left. Where are the people working?

Image 4 of 5

Baby Roosevelt and the snakes

Not done

What you’re looking at: A color cartoon from 1906 in Norton Ch. 20. A baby with a mustache and round glasses grabs two snakes with human heads, one in each hand. Norton says the baby is President Theodore Roosevelt. The cartoon compares him to the Greek hero Hercules, who strangled snakes when he was a baby.

Heads up: This cartoon makes fun of real people, and the faces are exaggerated. Aim your joke at the baby, the snakes, or the big fight. Never joke about how any person looks.

  • What is the baby doing? What is wrapped around him?
  • Does the cartoonist seem to be on the baby’s side or on the snakes’ side? How can you tell?

Image 5 of 5

Alice Paul sews a suffrage flag

Not done

What you’re looking at: A black-and-white photograph from Norton Ch. 20. A woman sits in a wicker chair and sews a large flag with rows of stars that covers her lap. Norton says she is Alice Paul and that suffragists often waved flags like this one during strikes and protests.

Heads up: This is a real person who worked for the right to vote. Aim your joke at the huge flag, the wicker chair, or how long sewing takes. Never joke about Alice Paul, other women, or anyone who was arrested.

  • What is she doing? What do you see on the flag?
  • Norton says suffragists waved flags like this at strikes and protests. Why would a flag help a protest?
